title: Teaching and supervision
text:
I am examiner, course coordinator and main teacher for two Master’s-level courses.



TMMV59 · 6 credits · Master’s level
Practical training in CFD for complex flow and heat transfer problems: the full workflow from modelling strategy, choice of physical models and numerical methods, and meshing to verification and validation. Students also learn to manage simulation projects, assess errors and uncertainties, automate workflows for high-performance computing, and communicate results. The course combines lectures, workshops, computer exercises and project work with input from industry.
Course page at LiU



TMMV64 · 6 credits · Master’s level
Data-driven modelling and machine learning for mechanical engineering. Students process, analyse and visualise data from mechanical and energy systems and implement predictive and classification models in Python. Lectures and hands-on labs end in a project that applies the methods to a real engineering problem.
Course page at LiU

title: Research
text: My research combines computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with data science and machine learning to understand, predict and control complex flows. I aim for methods that are efficient, robust and general enough to be used beyond canonical test cases, and I apply them to problems ranging from canonical flows to engineering systems such as turbomachinery. Most of the methods are developed in OpenFOAM and released as open-source software.

title: Research
text:
Reinforcement-learning-based flow control
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can discover feedback control strategies for nonlinear flows that are hard to design with classical methods. Current DRL–CFD frameworks, however, struggle with efficiency, robustness and generalisation. My work pushes DRL towards realistic flows by combining it with multi-fidelity learning, transfer learning and robust learning under uncertainty.
I developed an intrusive DRL framework in which the agent runs inside the OpenFOAM solver, avoiding external data exchange during training and running parallel environments with MPI. It has been applied to vortex shedding behind 2D and 3D cylinders and to the vortex rope in a swirl generator, a simplified model of a turbine draft tube. The ongoing ÅForsk project extends this to realistic hydraulic turbines.
Key work

S. Salehi, An efficient intrusive deep reinforcement learning framework for OpenFOAM, Meccanica, 2025
S. Salehi, Transfer learning strategies for accelerating reinforcement-learning-based flow control, arXiv preprint, 2025
S. Salehi and H. Nilsson, A parametric study of axial flow jets for mitigation of vortex rope instabilities, IOP Conf. Ser.: Earth Environ. Sci., 2025

Software: TensorforceFoam · agentJet

title: Research
text:
Transient operation of hydraulic turbines
Start-up, shutdown and load changes are becoming frequent as hydropower balances intermittent wind and solar power, and they expose turbines to strong pressure pulsations. Simulating them requires the mesh to follow moving guide vanes and runner blades. I developed a semi-implicit slip algorithm for mesh deformation in complex geometries, implemented in OpenFOAM, and used it for resolved simulations of Francis and Kaplan turbines during transient operation.
These simulations reveal how flow instabilities such as the rotating vortex rope form and decay during transients. The mesh-motion library is released as open source and is used by the R&D department of Vattenfall to study transient operation of their hydropower systems.
Key work

S. Salehi, H. Nilsson, E. Lillberg and N. Edh, An in-depth numerical analysis of transient flow field in a Francis turbine during shutdown, Renewable Energy, 2021
S. Salehi and H. Nilsson, Flow-induced pulsations in Francis turbines during startup, Renewable Energy, 2022
S. Salehi and H. Nilsson, A semi-implicit slip algorithm for mesh deformation in complex geometries, implemented in OpenFOAM, Computer Physics Communications, 2023
F. A. Masoodi, S. Salehi and R. Goyal, Reorganization of flow field due to load rejection driven self-mitigation of high load vortex breakdown in a Francis turbine, Physics of Fluids, 2024

Software: semiImplicitSlip · Francis-99 transients

title: Research
text:
Modal analysis and reduced-order modelling
High-fidelity simulations produce large, detailed data sets. Modal decompositions such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), spectral POD, dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) and sparsity-promoting DMD extract the coherent structures and dominant frequencies hidden in them. I have used these methods to analyse the vortex rope in hydraulic turbines, identifying the modes that govern the instability. This is a basis for reduced-order models and for designing control strategies.
Key work

S. Salehi and H. Nilsson, Modal analysis of vortex rope using dynamic mode decomposition, Physics of Fluids, 2024
S. Salehi and H. Nilsson, Dynamic mode decomposition of rotating vortex rope instability, 9th IAHR Meeting of the Work Group on Cavitation and Dynamic Problems in Hydraulic Machinery and Systems, 2024

title: Research
text:
Physics-informed neural networks
Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) embed the governing equations in the loss function of a neural network. Together with colleagues at Chalmers University of Technology, I study multi-fidelity PINNs for solving partial differential equations, with applications to the linear wave problem from potential flow theory, comparing soft and hard enforcement of boundary conditions. This work is the PhD project of Mohammad Sheikholeslami, whom I co-supervise.
Key work

M. Sheikholeslami, S. Salehi, W. Mao, A. Eslamdoost and H. Nilsson, Physics-informed neural networks with hard and soft boundary conditions for linear free surface waves, Physics of Fluids, 2025

title: Research
text:
Uncertainty quantification
In my doctoral research I developed efficient uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for turbulent and industrial flows. Sparse polynomial chaos with compressed sensing, and a multi-fidelity ℓ₁-minimisation method, reduce the number of expensive CFD simulations needed while retaining accuracy. Applied to hydraulic pumps, the methods showed that combined operational and geometrical uncertainties significantly affect flow and performance. They were also used for probabilistic CFD and robust optimisation of a cooled gas turbine vane.

title: Research
section: Flexible hydropower: loads, lifetime and energy storage
text:
Flexible hydropower: loads, lifetime and energy storage
Together with PhD students at Chalmers University of Technology, I study how flexible operation affects hydropower machines. CFD of a Kaplan turbine model shows how flow-induced forces, pressure pulsations and rotating vortex rope dynamics load the runner at part load and during load reduction, giving input for fatigue lifetime analysis (PhD student Martina Nobilo). In the EU Horizon 2020 project ALPHEUS we studied contra-rotating pump-turbines for low-head pumped hydro storage, including start-up and shutdown sequences and cavitating conditions (PhD student Jonathan Fahlbeck).

title: Enabling Flexible Hydropower Operation by AI-Based Active Flow Control
text:
Project summary
This project investigates AI-based active flow control for mitigating harmful flow instabilities in hydraulic turbines operating under off-design conditions. By coupling Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) with high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), the project aims to create a feedback-driven control framework that stabilizes the flow across varying operating regimes, contributing to safer and more flexible hydropower operation.



Conceptual illustration of the project. An AI agent observes the flow in the turbine draft tube and learns to actively control the instability through jet actuation.


The project is funded by the ÅForsk Foundation through an Early-Career Research Grant, with co-funding from Linköping University.
Principal investigator: Saeed Salehi, Linköping University
Co-supervisor: Håkan Nilsson, Chalmers University of Technology
The project is carried out as a collaboration between the Division of Applied Thermodynamics and Fluid Mechanics at Linköping University and the Division of Fluid Dynamics at Chalmers University of Technology.

title: Enabling Flexible Hydropower Operation by AI-Based Active Flow Control
text:
Background and motivation
The increasing penetration of intermittent energy sources such as wind and solar power places greater demands on hydropower to operate more flexibly to balance the electric grid. This flexible operation involves frequent starts and stops, continuous regulation, and prolonged operation at off-design conditions. These operations are known to promote strong self-induced flow instabilities that generate harmful pressure pulsations (Salehi and Nilsson, 2021; Salehi and Nilsson, 2022), accelerate structural fatigue, reduce lifetime, and limit the safe operating range of hydraulic turbines (Nobilo et al., 2026).



Flow instability during shutdown operation of a Francis turbine, showing helical vortex rope structures in the draft tube (Salehi and Nilsson, 2021).


Several strategies have been proposed to mitigate flow instabilities in hydraulic turbines. Passive approaches rely on geometric modifications of the runner or draft tube to weaken instabilities or stabilize the flow. Active flow control techniques typically employ air admission or water injection supplied by external energy sources. Air admission redistributes low-pressure regions to damp pulsations, whereas water injection directly alters the angular momentum of the swirling flow.
Despite the progress in passive and active mitigation strategies, most reported approaches rely on predefined geometric modifications or actuation settings tailored to specific operating conditions, without adaptive feedback from the evolving flow field. While these strategies may reduce pressure fluctuations and their associated vibrations, their performance is limited to specific operating regimes and is sensitive to tuning. In addition, most active control strategies do not explicitly account for performance optimality; instability mitigation is often achieved at the expense of increased actuation energy or reduced turbine efficiency.
These limitations motivate the development of feedback-based control strategies that maintain effective instability mitigation across varying operating conditions while minimizing additional energy consumption and limiting turbine efficiency degradation. This is the main purpose of this project.

title: Enabling Flexible Hydropower Operation by AI-Based Active Flow Control
text:
Approach
The high-dimensional and nonlinear dynamics of turbine instabilities limit the practical applicability of conventional model-based control methods. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers an alternative by enabling systematic optimization of control policies directly from flow observations in complex dynamical systems. Recent advances in DRL have demonstrated the ability to construct feedback control policies for complex, nonlinear flow systems, including laminar (Rabault et al., 2019), weakly turbulent (Ren et al., 2021), and fully turbulent flows (Sonoda et al., 2023), though predominantly in simplified settings rather than realistic engineering systems.
In the proposed framework, a deep neural network (the agent) interacts with a high-fidelity CFD simulation in a closed loop: the agent observes the flow state, selects a control action (e.g., jet actuation), and receives a reward signal reflecting the degree of instability suppression. Through iterative training, the agent learns a control policy that adapts to the flow dynamics, without requiring an explicit mathematical model of the instability.
With DRL-based flow control showing promising results in canonical configurations, extending these approaches to practical engineering systems such as turbine instability problems is a logical next step.

title: Enabling Flexible Hydropower Operation by AI-Based Active Flow Control
text:
Previous research
The project builds on previous work in high-fidelity simulation of hydraulic turbine flows and reinforcement learning-based flow control. Much of this groundwork was carried out while the PI was a researcher at Chalmers University of Technology, funded by the Swedish Centre for Sustainable Hydropower (SVC).

High-fidelity simulation of hydraulic turbines
Previous work includes high-fidelity simulations of hydraulic turbines under steady, off-design, and transient operations, covering vortex rope dynamics, shutdown and start-up transients, and uncertainty quantification in Francis turbines, Kaplan turbines, pump-turbines, and swirl generator configurations (e.g., Salehi and Nilsson, 2021; Salehi and Nilsson, 2022; Salehi and Nilsson, 2023; Salehi and Nilsson, 2024; Masoodi et al., 2024a; Masoodi et al., 2024b).


DRL-CFD coupling framework
In parallel, we have developed a computational framework for coupling DRL with the CFD solver OpenFOAM (Salehi, 2025). The framework enables efficient closed-loop integration between learning algorithms and high-fidelity flow simulations and has been released as open-source software: TensorforceFoam on GitHub.
The methodology has been applied to active flow control problems. The figures below illustrate representative results, including successful control of vortex-dominated flow structures in both 2D and 3D configurations.



Uncontrolled (left) and DRL-controlled (right) flow past a 2D cylinder (Salehi, 2025). The learned control policy suppresses the vortex shedding.








Uncontrolled 3D cylinder wake







DRL-controlled 3D cylinder wake







Proof-of-concept: DRL control of draft tube instability
As a first step toward the present project, we conducted a proof-of-concept study on a swirl generator configuration representing a simplified hydraulic turbine draft tube. A DRL controller was coupled to a 3D CFD model with localized axial jet actuation at the runner cone.






Uncontrolled vortex rope







DRL-controlled vortex rope





Under closed-loop control, the strength of the helical flow instability is reduced compared to the uncontrolled case. The corresponding time evolution of the rotating pressure mode is shown below. When the controller is activated at \(t = 1\) s (dashed red line), the rotating mode amplitude decreases and stabilizes at a lower level.



Time evolution of the rotating pressure mode. The DRL controller is activated at \(t = 1\) s (dashed red line), after which the pressure oscillation amplitude is rapidly suppressed.


This preliminary study considered a simplified geometry, a single operating condition, and a basic actuation setup to establish feasibility. Extending this framework to realistic turbine configurations, multiple operating regimes, advanced actuator concepts, and higher-fidelity simulations is the next step and constitutes the core of this project.

title: Enabling Flexible Hydropower Operation by AI-Based Active Flow Control
section: What is new in this project
text:
What is new in this project
To date, no DRL-based closed-loop control framework has been applied to instability mitigation in realistic hydraulic turbine configurations. This project aims to fill that gap by integrating DRL directly with high-fidelity CFD of turbines, moving beyond predefined geometric modifications and open-loop actuation toward regime-robust, efficiency-aware control across off-design operating conditions.

MSc and BSc thesis projects
I supervise thesis projects in areas such as:

development of CFD methods in OpenFOAM
high-fidelity simulation of turbulent and unsteady flows
data-driven and machine learning methods for flow analysis and control

If you study at Linköping University and would like to align your thesis with my research, feel free to contact me.

title: Opportunities
text:
PhD positions
A PhD position on AI-based active flow control for hydraulic turbines, funded by the ÅForsk Foundation, was advertised in 2026. The application period closed on 31 August 2026, and assessment and recruitment are under way. We received a large number of applications, so this will take some time. Thank you to all applicants for your patience. Read about the project.
New funded positions will be announced here and on the Linköping University vacancies page.

title: Opportunities
text:
Postdocs and fellowships
There are no funded postdoc openings at the moment. If you have your own funding or plan to apply for a fellowship, I am happy to discuss possible projects. I will support strong applications for external scholarships and fellowships and can host you at Linköping University.


Examples of funding for PhD candidates

Swedish national graduate schools (e.g. WASP)

Other national or EU-funded PhD scholarship programmes

title: Opportunities
text:
How to get in touch
If you are interested in joining, email me with:

a short CV
a brief description of your research interests and how they connect to my research
your background in CFD, programming and machine learning
if relevant, your plan for applying for a scholarship or external funding

title: Software
text: I release the methods I develop as open-source code, so that they can be used and checked by both academic and industrial users. Most of the projects extend OpenFOAM. All code is on GitHub.

title: Software
text:
Reinforcement learning and flow control

TensorforceFoam
An intrusive deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for OpenFOAM, built on TensorFlow and the Tensorforce package. Intrusive means the DRL agent is integrated directly into the CFD environment, so no external information exchange is needed during DRL episodes. Parallel environments for expensive CFD cases are handled through MPI (mpi4py).
Code on GitHub · Paper: Salehi, Meccanica, 2025


agentJet
An OpenFOAM boundary condition that deploys a trained DRL policy as a jet actuator directly inside the CFD solver. The saved TensorFlow policy is evaluated through the TensorFlow C++ API (cppflow), so no Python coupling is needed at run time. At each control period the flow state is sampled at probe locations, and the policy returns a jet velocity that is ramped smoothly from the previous action.
Code on GitHub

title: Software
text:
Hydraulic turbines and mesh motion

semiImplicitSlip
A mesh-motion library for OpenFOAM with a robust semi-implicit algorithm for slipping mesh points along curved surfaces: an explicit step based on the general slip condition followed by an implicit step based on a Dirichlet condition, with Laplacian smoothing to spread the deformation into the domain. A solid-body rotation can be added on top, for example to model the runner of a Kaplan turbine during transient operation.
Code on GitHub · Paper: Salehi and Nilsson, Computer Physics Communications, 2023


Francis-99 transients
Open case files and code for CFD simulation of the transient operation of a Francis turbine in OpenFOAM.
Dataset on Harvard Dataverse · Paper: Salehi and Nilsson, OpenFOAM Journal, 2021


OpenFOAM-Swirl-Number
A pipeline for computing the swirl number, the ratio of the axial flux of angular momentum to the axial flux of axial momentum, in OpenFOAM. Modular function objects extract and transform the velocity field and integrate the momentum fluxes over a sampled cross-section. A Python script then computes and plots the swirl number over time.
Code on GitHub

title: Software
text:
Teaching

OSCFD
Test codes and examples for the PhD course CFD with Open-Source Software at Chalmers University of Technology, complementing lectures on memory management in C++ and OpenFOAM. They range from standalone C++ examples (dynamic allocation, copy semantics, smart pointers) to OpenFOAM applications that examine autoPtr and tmp.
Code on GitHub
